item.title: OpenAI countersues Apple, accusing it of stealing trade secrets
item.description:
The legal fight between Apple and OpenAI escalated sharply this week, with OpenAI filing a countersuit accusing Apple of stealing its trade secrets and threatening suppliers that work with both companies. Apple's original lawsuit, filed in July, alleged that former Apple employees who defected to OpenAI took confidential information with them; Apple says OpenAI has already been ordered to stop using it.

OpenAI's complaint paints a vivid picture of Apple's employment practices, claiming Apple 'set quite a trap for employees' and quoting the Eagles' 'Hotel California': 'you can check out any time you like, but you can never leave.' Apple dismissed the counterclaims as 'a transparent attempt to distract from the substance of Apple's lawsuit.' The case is still in its earliest stages, but it is now a two-way trade-secrets battle between two of the most powerful companies in tech.

Sources

  • AppleInsider News: OpenAI counter-sues Apple over trade secret theft
  • Daring Fireball: OpenAI Countersues Apple for Stealing Trade Secrets
  • 9to5Mac: OpenAI countersues Apple, alleging trade secret theft and supplier threats; Apple responds

item.title: Chile sues Apple over App Store rules, seeking an $80 million fine
item.description:
Chile's national competition authority, the Fiscalía Nacional Económica (FNE), has filed an antitrust lawsuit against Apple, accusing the company of abusing its dominant position in iOS app distribution and in-app purchases. The regulator is asking the country's antitrust court to fine Apple approximately $80 million and impose corrective measures, including opening iOS to alternative app stores and payment systems.

According to the filing, Apple has restricted competition in both areas since at least 2021. Apple has responded to the suit. It's the latest in a growing line of App Store antitrust fights around the world, adding pressure on Apple to loosen its grip on how iPhone apps are distributed and paid for.

Sources

  • 9to5Mac: Apple faces potential $80 million fine and App Store overhaul in Chile [U: Apple responds]
  • AppleInsider News: Apple faces another App Store antitrust fight, this time in Chile

item.title: Three more iPhones coming in early 2027 — but production is running late
item.description:
Apple's split iPhone launch cycle continues into next year, with the standard iPhone 18, iPhone 18e, and iPhone Air 2 all expected in early 2027, likely February or March. The iPhone Air 2 is shaping up to get the most substantial changes of the three, reportedly including a 48-megapixel camera upgrade.

But the schedule looks tight. Leaker Fixed Focus Digital reports that neither the iPhone 18 nor the iPhone 18e has entered mass production yet, with the start pushed back from late October to around New Year's Day 2027 — months behind Apple's usual timeline. That leaves little slack before the spring launch window, though reports still expect Apple to hit its February or March target.

Carriers piled on too, with up to $1,200 off the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo plus free Apple gear with qualifying purchases, and Apple TV at $6.99 a month for six months. Apple's own shopping event was more modest, offering gift cards of up to $300 with eligible purchases rather than cash discounts.

item.title: (PRODUCT)RED HomePod mini 2 spotted in stores ahead of December 1 launch
item.description:
The rumored (PRODUCT)RED version of the HomePod mini 2 has seemingly been spotted on display at a few stores before it is officially announced. Photos shared on X and Reddit show the speaker with a red mesh finish and what appears to be a (PRODUCT)RED label on the box. Bloomberg had reported earlier this week that Apple was gearing up to launch Product(RED) versions of select products.

The speaker is expected to be released by Tuesday, December 1, which is World AIDS Day — the traditional launch date for Apple's (RED) products. No other changes are expected beyond the new color. The sighting suggests Apple is ready to announce it any day now.

item.title: iPhone grabs 57% of the US market and dominates China's Singles' Day
item.description:
Apple had a standout quarter in smartphones on both sides of the Pacific. In the US, iPhone's share of the market jumped from 50% to 57% in the third quarter of 2026, according to Counterpoint Research — even as overall US smartphone shipments fell 9% year over year. Apple was the only major manufacturer to avoid a shipment decline, while Samsung held its ground at 25%.

In China, Apple led smartphone sales during this year's Double 11 shopping festival, claiming six of the country's 10 bestselling smartphones despite a broader slump in demand. Counterpoint attributes the wider market weakness in part to rising memory costs, which have hit Android manufacturers hardest at the low end, where thin margins leave little room to absorb higher component prices.

Sources

  • 9to5Mac: Apple claims six of China's 10 bestselling smartphones during Singles' Day

item.title: iOS 27.3 will put daily limits on advanced AI features
item.description:
iOS 27.3, launching next month alongside macOS 27.3, will introduce daily usage limits on certain advanced Apple Intelligence features, according to leaker 'pdfu' posting on X. Apple has not said precisely which features are capped or what the thresholds will be — but the change suggests Apple is starting to meter its most compute-heavy AI capabilities rather than offering them without restriction.

The update arrives on the heels of iOS 27.2, which added two improvements for CarPlay users, and macOS 27.3 is set to bring three new features to the Mac at the same time. Taken together, the releases point to a steady cadence of software refinements as Apple balances expanding its AI ambitions with the cost of running them.

item.title: Apple TV unveils Neuromancer and wins an International Emmy for 'Carême'
item.description:
Apple TV is lining up its next big sci-fi bet: Neuromancer, an adaptation of William Gibson's landmark cyberpunk novel. A new behind-the-scenes piece reveals fresh details about the series, which Apple is positioning as a potential Severance- or Pluribus-sized hit for the streamer. It arrives as Apple TV is running a Black Friday promotion at $6.99 a month for new and returning subscribers.

Meanwhile, Apple TV picked up more awards hardware this week: its French-language drama 'Carême' won Best Drama Series at the 54th International Emmy Awards, Apple's second win in the category after 'Drops of God' in 2024. The series follows a chef whose culinary ambitions draw him into espionage in Napoleon's France, and a second season is already in production.

item.title: South Korea opens formal case over allegedly misleading Apple Intelligence ads
item.description:
South Korea's Fair Trade Commission has opened formal proceedings against Apple over how it advertised Apple Intelligence features for the iPhone 16 lineup. Investigators allege Apple misled consumers about which features were actually available at launch, pointing to Genmoji, Image Playground, and Siri's promised ability to understand personal context and onscreen awareness — features that arrived late or, in some cases, still haven't shipped as advertised.

The question is whether Apple adequately explained the timing: what buyers would get on day one versus what was coming later. It's the latest regulatory headache over AI marketing claims, and it lands as Apple Intelligence remains a work in progress more than a year after the iPhone 16 launched with it as a headline feature.

Sources

  • 9to5Mac: South Korea proceeds with case over allegedly misleading Apple Intelligence ads
  • MacRumors: Apple Faces Korean Regulator Review Over iPhone 16 AI Advertising

item.title: Judge orders Apple to hand over 3,200 documents in Epic Games dispute
item.description:
A federal judge has ordered Apple to produce a random sample of 3,200 documents for Epic Games to review, after Epic alleged Apple improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions. The sampled documents will let Epic test whether Apple's withholding was justified — a key question in the long-running fight over how Apple charges developers for purchases made outside the App Store.

The order keeps the Epic saga alive well after the headline rulings, and it matters because the commission rules at stake affect every developer selling through iOS. If the sample shows Apple held back material it shouldn't have, expect Epic to push for broader disclosure and potentially harsher consequences.

Sources

  • 9to5Mac: Judge orders Apple to produce 3,200 documents in Epic Games dispute

item.title: Apple took 57% of US smartphone shipments in Q3 — the only major maker to grow
item.description:
Apple's share of US smartphone shipments jumped from 50% to 57% year over year last quarter, and it was the only major smartphone maker to buck a broader decline in shipments. The iPhone 17 and 18 lineups appear to be driving the surge, with Apple consolidating its already-dominant position in its home market.

The number is striking less for the growth itself than for the concentration: well over half of all smartphones shipped in the US last quarter were iPhones. For rivals, that means competing for a shrinking slice of the market, and for Apple it reinforces how much of its business now depends on keeping iPhone demand strong cycle after cycle.

Sources

  • 9to5Mac: Report: Apple accounted for 57% of US smartphone shipments in Q3

item.title: iOS 28 reportedly set to revamp iPhone notifications
item.description:
iOS 28, due next year, will reportedly include a revamp of the iPhone's notification system. Details are thin — the rumor says only that Apple plans significant changes — but the timing is notable: Android has recently added tools like a Notification Organizer to help users sort alerts into categories, and notification overload has become a common complaint on both platforms.

The open question is what kind of revamp this is: smarter grouping and filtering, or more of Apple's own promotional notifications, which it already occasionally sends. Given how central notifications are to daily iPhone use, even a modest redesign would be one of the more consequential changes in iOS 28 — for better or worse.

Sources

  • 9to5Mac: iOS 28 to 'revamp' iPhone notifications, per report
  • AppleInsider: iOS 28 will either fix notification abuse or make it all worse

item.title: Sketchy rumor: a limited-edition ceramic iPhone 20 Pro
item.description:
A rumor from Weibo leaker Fixed Focus Digital — a source with a mixed track record — claims Apple has ceramic components in hand for the 20th-anniversary iPhone 20 Pro, expected next year. Planned production capacity is reportedly very low, suggesting a limited-edition model, and the project would only reach mass production if it passes engineering validation testing.

Treat this one with heavy skepticism: there are no details on what the ceramic parts actually are, and the most consistent reporting says the iPhone 20 Pro will borrow design elements from the iPhone Air, including more rounded glass. Still, a ceramic anniversary edition would fit Apple's pattern of marking milestones with a special model — and it gives the rumor mill something to chew on until the phone is closer to launch.

Sources

  • MacRumors: iPhone 20 Pro Could Feature Ceramic in Limited-Edition Model

item.title: Apple still working on a giant foldable iPad that could cost up to $5,000
item.description:
Apple is still developing a large foldable iPad despite ongoing technical challenges and uncertainty over whether it will ever ship, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman. The device, known internally as Project J312, would have a display of around 19 to 20 inches — Gurman described it as resembling a "gigantic iPhone Duo with no display on the outside" — and could cost between $3,000 and $5,000.

Apple originally hoped to announce it by 2027, but that timeline has slipped. The project remains exploratory: a very expensive, very large foldable tablet is a niche product even by Apple's standards, and the engineering hurdles of a crease-free 20-inch folding display are real. For now it's a sign Apple hasn't abandoned the idea — not a promise it will ever reach stores.

Sources

  • MacRumors: Apple Still Working on Giant Foldable iPad That Could Cost $5,000

item.title: iPhones dominated China's weak Singles' Day phone sales
item.description:
Apple held the top spot in China's smartphone market during the Singles' Day shopping festival, despite an 8% year-over-year sales decline, according to Counterpoint Research. The overall market fell 17% across the promotional period, and six of the top 10 bestsellers were iPhone 17 and 18 models, led by the iPhone 18 Pro Max, with the iPhone Duo at No. 9.

The context is a soft market, not an Apple problem: buyers are postponing upgrades instead of accepting higher prices after strong iPhone 18 Pro launch sales. Huawei was the only major brand to grow in the period, rising 29%. Apple's lead in a shrinking market underscores how much of the premium segment it now owns in China — but also how dependent it is on convincing buyers to upgrade on schedule.

Sources

  • MacRumors: iPhones Dominate China's Weak Singles' Day Smartphone Sales

item.title: 1Password breach exposed customer names and emails — vaults untouched
item.description:
1Password disclosed a security incident in which an attacker breached an employee's GitHub account on November 19, used it to access source code, and pushed malicious code to backend services that copied a limited amount of customer account information — names and email addresses used to sign in — from a subset of customers.

The company stresses that vault contents and the keys protecting them were not affected, and it says it does not have access to users' passwords or secret keys. It has contained the incident, restored clean versions of the affected service, and rotated internal credentials. Customers don't need to change anything, but 1Password is warning everyone to watch for phishing attempts using the stolen contact details — a realistic risk, since attackers now know who uses the service and how to reach them.

item.title: Apple pulls AI companion app Talkie after child-safety investigation
item.description:
Apple removed the popular AI companion app Talkie from the App Store on Wednesday after reports that its characters sent inappropriate messages to minors. Apple cited sexual content as the reason for removal, but an investigation by The Bureau of Investigative Journalism suggests the violations went further and involved minors.

The case highlights a recurring problem with AI companion apps: chatbots designed for roleplay will generally go along with whatever they're asked, and age gates are the main line of defense. Talkie was easily findable on the App Store, and the episode raises fresh questions about how thoroughly Apple vets AI apps whose core feature is open-ended conversation with users.

Sources

  • AppleInsider News: AI chatbot companion app Talkie pulled from Apple App Store after investigation
  • 9to5Mac: Apple pulls popular Chinese AI chatbot from the App Store amid child safety concerns

item.title: 32 states and major developers back Epic in Apple's Supreme Court appeal
item.description:
Epic Games has picked up heavyweight backing in Apple's Supreme Court appeal of the civil contempt ruling in the long-running Epic v. Apple case. Thirty-two states plus the District of Columbia filed in support of Epic, joined by major developers, legal experts, and former federal judges.

The appeal centers on the contempt finding against Apple over its compliance with the court order requiring it to allow developers to link out to alternative payment options. The breadth of support — state attorneys general as well as industry voices — signals that the case is now seen as much bigger than a dispute between two companies, with the outcome likely to shape how much control Apple can keep over App Store payments and developer communications.

Sources

  • 9to5Mac: Major developers, legal experts, and 32 states back Epic in Apple’s SCOTUS appeal

item.title: Big MacBook Air overhaul with OLED may land in 2027 or 2028
item.description:
Apple's most popular computer is in line for a major redesign, but buyers shouldn't expect it soon. Bloomberg's Mark Gurman said on his Power On podcast that a MacBook Air with a new look could launch in late 2027 or 2028, possibly gaining an OLED display at that point — a significant upgrade for a machine that has kept the same basic design for years.

Before that, Apple plans a more modest refresh in early 2027, with M6 chips arriving in the MacBook Air alongside the MacBook Neo 2, but no new design. So anyone shopping for a MacBook Air in the near term is looking at a spec bump, while the real overhaul — new design, likely OLED — is still at least a year away.

item.title: Apple has iPads running macOS internally — but don't get excited
item.description:
Apple has iPads running macOS internally and has had them "for some time," according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, but there is no work underway to bring the Mac operating system to iPads as a consumer product. The experiment exists; the product doesn't.

Instead, Apple will keep bringing Mac features and apps to iPadOS piece by piece — Final Cut Pro being the latest example. Gurman also noted that per-operating-system EU regulation gives Apple an incentive to keep the two systems distinct. The long-running dream of a macOS iPad remains just that, though the existence of working internal builds, plus the new touchscreen MacBook Pro, keeps the speculation alive.

item.title: Apple has an iPhone notifications problem — and iOS 28 may revamp the system
item.description:
Apple's App Store guidelines say apps may only send promotional push notifications if users explicitly opt in, with a clear way to opt out — but some apps are flouting those rules, and Apple doesn't appear to be enforcing them consistently. Users are getting ads through notifications and Live Activities they never agreed to, with little recourse.

There may be relief coming: multiple sources say Apple plans to revamp the iPhone's notification system with iOS 28 next year, with significant changes to Notification Center, though no specifics have leaked. Android 16 already filters notifications into categories like News, Promotions, and Social, and an equivalent on iOS would give users real control over the flood. For now it's a rumor, but it lands alongside a genuine enforcement gap.

Sources

  • MacRumors: Apple Has an iPhone Notifications Problem
  • MacRumors: Rumor: iOS 28 to Revamp Notifications

item.title: New tariffs target Apple's main iPhone manufacturing countries
item.description:
The tariff saga is escalating again for Apple. A new set of tariffs affecting 14 trading partners has been proposed, hitting imports from India, China, Taiwan, Mexico, and more — effectively all of Apple's main iPhone manufacturing countries.

Tariffs have been a running cost and supply-chain headache for Apple throughout the Trump presidencies, and this round targets the very countries where iPhones are assembled. Details of the rates and timing remain thin, but the direction is clear: Apple faces another round of pressure on its manufacturing footprint, and the costs could eventually show up in pricing or in further shifts of where devices are built.

item.title: Walmart drops Apple Pay from its app and website after just weeks
item.description:
Walmart has quietly removed Apple Pay from its website and iPhone app, just weeks after finally adding it. Walmart was one of Apple Pay's longest-running holdouts since its 2014 launch, forcing shoppers to use its own Walmart Pay QR codes instead — a setup that gave the retailer more insight into customer habits. It relented in August 2026, rolling out Apple Pay online and, separately, tap-to-pay in stores.

No reason was given, and some users may still see the option, raising the possibility of A/B testing. In-store Apple Pay still works. For now, online Walmart shoppers are back to cards and Walmart Pay — a strange step backward from a retailer that only just ended a decade of resistance.

item.title: iPhone 18e and iPhone Air 2 leaks show redesigned, thicker camera bumps
item.description:
CAD files seen by Engadget suggest next year's budget and thin iPhones both get camera redesigns. The iPhone 18e would trade the 17e's nearly flush single lens — flash and microphone sitting separately in the rear glass — for a raised, almost square plateau, about 28 by 35 millimeters, housing the camera, flash, and microphone together, in a style compared to the M5 iPad Pro.

The iPhone Air 2 is shown with two rear cameras side by side, and its camera plateau grows from 3.45mm to 3.8mm thick while the body stays 5.6mm. That matches dummy models shared last week, with both lenses toward the left of the plateau and flash and mic on the right. As with all CAD leaks, the designs could still change before launch.

item.title: Apple hands Epic less than 1% of required documents in App Store fee fight
item.description:
The years-long Apple vs. Epic legal saga has a new flashpoint: document production. In a November 23 filing in federal court in California, Epic claims Apple has handed over less than 1% of the documents required in the current phase of the fight, which centers on the commission Apple charges on purchases made through outbound links. Epic says Apple agreed to a schedule and is failing to meet it; the court apparently agrees there are red flags.

It's the latest chapter in a case that began with Fortnite's removal from the App Store and has since sprawled across fees, steering rules, and court-order compliance. No ruling has been reported yet, but the court's skepticism suggests Apple may be forced to produce far more, far faster.

Sources

item.title: EU in talks with Apple over barriers to rival iPhone browsers
item.description:
The European Commission is in talks with Apple over iPhone browser rules, after Mozilla, Shopify, and a coalition representing up to 55,000 EU businesses and organizations published an open letter asking regulators to force a change. Google's Chrome team has now backed Mozilla's complaint, saying Apple's rules offer "choice on paper, not in practice."

Apple has technically allowed alternative browser engines in the EU since early 2024, but the coalition argues no browser maker has been able to actually migrate its EU users from Apple's WebKit engine to its own, because Apple's requirements make it too difficult in practice. Firefox on iPhone, for example, still runs on WebKit under the hood. The talks are the latest pressure point in the EU's ongoing effort to open up Apple's platforms.

Sources

item.title: iOS 27 changes how you open Notification Center — and adds Mail and Messages upgrades
item.description:
iOS 27 changes a gesture iPhone and iPad users have relied on since iOS 5 in 2011: how you open Notification Center. The new behavior shipped after shifting slightly between the early releases, and even seasoned users report they're still adjusting — fifteen years of muscle memory doesn't rewire overnight.

Elsewhere in iOS 27, Apple Mail picked up four new features, Messages gained a long-requested setting to customize or turn off the audio button, and iPhone Handoff — which lets you use the same phone number across two iPhones — is rolling out with carrier support varying by provider. If something in your daily iPhone routine feels off after updating, one of these changes is probably the culprit.

item.title: Claude can now turn artifacts into semi-independent Mac apps
item.description:
Anthropic has given Claude a new trick: it can now build macOS apps from prompts, turning its interactive artifacts into semi-independent desktop apps on Mac (and Windows). It's the furthest any major AI assistant has gone toward letting anyone vibe-code a real app, and it follows Apple's own move into agentic coding with Xcode 27.

But there's a major caveat. These AI-generated apps lack the review, sandboxing, and signing guarantees of App Store software, and AppleInsider's take is blunt: the feature makes building a Mac app look easier than ever, but the resulting apps are worth avoiding altogether. Fun to experiment with, risky to actually run — treat anything Claude builds as untrusted code.

item.title: Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO after Trump intervenes
item.description:
Nvidia's board voted unanimously to reinstate Jensen Huang as president and CEO effective immediately, less than two weeks after he resigned on November 12 amid reports of extramarital affairs. The board said it was satisfied with Huang's candor and ability to lead after a series of meetings, and noted it had received input from senior levels of the U.S. government and was confident his return poses no national security risk.

The reversal followed direct intervention from President Trump, who called into a board meeting hours before the vote to argue for Huang's return and later said Huang "did nothing wrong." Nvidia's stock jumped more than 30% on the news, and employees greeted Huang's return to headquarters with chants as he apologized for "putting all of you through all of this." The episode caps a remarkable about-face: the board had previously said it had no intention of reinstating him.

item.title: 55,000 EU businesses urge crackdown on Apple's iPhone browser rules
item.description:
A coalition led by Mozilla and Shopify, representing up to 55,000 European businesses and organizations, is urging the European Commission to open formal enforcement proceedings against Apple over iPhone browser competition.

In an open letter to Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, the group argues that Apple's changes under the Digital Markets Act have failed to deliver real browser choice. More than two and a half years after the DMA took effect, no browser vendor has managed to move its existing EU users off Apple's WebKit engine to its own engine, the coalition says, because Apple's rules still make switching effectively impractical. The letter also claims Apple's restrictions hamper selling subscriptions outside the App Store. The Commission has not yet said whether it will act.

item.title: Berkshire Hathaway keeps Apple as its biggest stock bet
item.description:
Berkshire Hathaway has stopped selling Apple shares, leaving the iPhone maker as its largest stock investment a decade after it first bought in. After selling down its stake through 2024 and 2025, Berkshire held its Apple position unchanged through September 2026 under its new CEO.

Warren Buffett first bought Apple in 2016, and the holding has long been Berkshire's biggest single bet — a vote of confidence that stands out as Berkshire has been actively trading the rest of its largest positions.

item.title: Google's AI search problem is costing Apple revenue
item.description:
Apple's Safari search deal with Google isn't as lucrative as it once was — and the cause isn't a falling-out between the two companies. Users are changing how they search, increasingly relying on AI answers instead of traditional search results, and Google's AI search isn't monetizing the way classic search did.

That matters because the deal, worth around $20 billion a year for Google to be Safari's default search engine, has been one of Apple's most profitable arrangements — and one that already drew a DOJ antitrust lawsuit. If AI changes search behavior faster than Google can monetize it, Apple's cut shrinks too. The shift in how people find information is quietly becoming a revenue problem for both companies.

item.title: Apple Intelligence gets paywalled tiers: iCloud+ buys more AI
item.description:
Apple has published a support document spelling out what was previously only implied: starting with the 2027 software releases, Siri AI and Apple Intelligence features are free on supported devices, but the server-powered features have usage limits — and higher limits come with paid iCloud+ plans, beginning with the 27.3 release. Affected features include Siri AI image tools like Clean Up, Extend, and Spatial Reframing, Image Playground, and the cloud models in Shortcuts workflows and automation.

This is the clearest sign yet that Apple is moving toward a freemium model for its most powerful AI features, with iCloud+ as the subscription lever. It's a notable shift from Apple's usual pitch of on-device, private AI, and it means heavy users of the cloud-backed tools will eventually hit a paywall — or a subscription prompt.

On the iPhone Duo, iOS 27.3 adds a facial unlock option — addressing one of the biggest complaints about the foldable, which launched without Apple's usual face-based authentication. Neither change is flashy, but both fix real annoyances: Duo owners finally get the unlock experience iPhone users expect, and Mac users get clearer guardrails over which apps can reach deep into their system. Expect the 27.3 releases to ship in the coming weeks as Apple wraps up its software year.
